AstroLogic

We are a team of developers and problem solvers participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our goal is to leverage software engineering, data analysis, and open-source NASA data to build meaningful solutions. Excited to innovate together!
summary: Open Case: Earth is a browser-based "planetary forensics" tool that turns thirty-five years of free NASA Earth data into a readable, testable case file for any place on Earth. Pick a location — or click the globe — and the app pulls the public NASA POWER monthly record, rebuilds annual and seasonal series, and asks the only question that matters: is this trend real, or is it noise? It answers with a plain-language verdict backed by Mann–Kendall significance corrected for serial correlation (Hamed–Rao), Sen's slope with a 95% interval, a 5×5 spatial grid collapsed to independent model cells under false-discovery control, four separate seasonal tests, and six robustness checks that set a printed grade — Established, Probable, Tentative or Unresolved. Solar and cloud are tested only from 2001, where the upstream satellite product changes, so a product step cannot pose as a trend. It then shows the same place from space across any two years of the MODIS record. It addresses "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" by making rigorous trend detection something anyone can open, read, and challenge in under a minute, with no account, no API key, and every formula visible. It matters because climate claims are everywhere, but the evidence behind them is usually locked inside code; this puts the evidence in public, place by place.
details:
What it does

Open Case: Earth opens a "case file" for any coordinate on Earth. For the selected place it reads the public NASA POWER monthly point record for eight Earth signals — air temperature, rainfall, root-zone soil wetness, solar radiation, cloud amount, humidity, wind speed and snow depth — and rebuilds clean annual and seasonal series for 1991–2025 against a 1991–2020 baseline. POWER serves several upstream NASA products through that one API, and the app names the product behind each signal: MERRA-2 reanalysis for temperature, rainfall, root-zone wetness and snow depth; MERRA-2 derived by POWER for humidity and wind speed; satellite radiation for solar irradiance and cloud amount. The radiation pair switches from GEWEX SRB to CERES SYN1deg in 2001, so those two signals are tested only over 2001–2025 against a 2001–2020 baseline: a step between two products is not a climate trend, and the app refuses to read it as one.

How it works

The analysis runs entirely in the browser. For the chosen signal it computes the Mann–Kendall trend test (with tie and continuity correction), Sen's median-of-pairwise-slopes estimate with a rank-based 95% confidence interval, and a least-squares cross-check. Climate years are not independent, so the test variance is corrected for serial correlation with the Hamed–Rao procedure on Sen-detrended residual ranks, and significance is judged on that corrected p. It then samples a 5×5 grid of neighbouring points, collapses samples that resolve to the same native model cell, and applies Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control once per independent cell, so an oversampled grid cannot count one cell as several pieces of evidence. The same false-discovery control runs across the eight signals at the point. Four meteorological seasons are tested separately (DJF uses the previous December), and six evidence checks — statistical signal, spatial agreement, seasonal agreement, record completeness, endpoint robustness and estimator agreement — combine into a single plain-language verdict such as "Significant warming" or "No clear trend", carrying a printed grade of Established, Probable, Tentative or Unresolved. A MODIS Terra true-colour compare slider shows the same place across any two years from 2000 to 2025 and any month, opening on 2002 against 2024, as visual context, and every case can be exported as a shareable PNG card with a QR code or downloaded as CSV.

Benefits

It makes the difference between a real trend and natural variability legible to non-specialists: students, journalists, planners and curious citizens can check a claim about their own home town in under a minute, see exactly which tests passed, and share the result. Because every formula and data source is displayed in an open method drawer, the verdict is auditable rather than a black box.

What we hope to achieve

A public habit of "show me the record": before repeating a climate claim, open the case for that place and read the evidence. The tool is deliberately honest about limits — every value is a grid-cell average rather than a station measurement, the radiation records are tested only inside the CERES era because the upstream product changes in 2001, the serial-correlation correction addresses persistence rather than a step change, and a non-significant result is reported as unresolved, not as proof of no change.

Tools and languages

TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, MapLibre GL JS (globe and spatial mosaic), Framer Motion, Lucide icons, Vitest (40 unit tests over the statistics, including regressions pinned against SciPy and pymannkendall), qrcode and html-to-image (shareable case cards), and self-hosted Fontsource typefaces (Instrument Serif, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono). Data: NASA POWER monthly point API (upstream MERRA-2, CERES SYN1deg, GEWEX SRB) and NASA GIBS (Blue Marble WMTS, MODIS Terra WMS). Place search: Photon / OpenStreetMap. No backend, no API keys, no account; deployed as a static site on Vercel. The complete source is public under the MIT licence: https://github.com/JinYi123456/open-case-earth

Use of Super Intelligence

SI (a large-language-model coding assistant) was used as an implementation accelerator under human direction: scaffolding and refactoring components, writing the statistics and data-fetching code, and debugging. The project idea, art direction and every scientific decision (which variables, which tests, which baseline, which thresholds) were made by the human team. No SI-generated imagery or video frames are used: all visuals are live screenshots of the running application or NASA satellite imagery. The demo narration is synthesized text-to-speech, acknowledged here and in the video description and metadata. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers are used or modified anywhere in the project.

Project demo format

The submitted Project Demo is the 7-slide presentation PDF at https://drive.google.com/file/d/1KkeWP_8FlC_Lky6Ak9QzxWuRPxcUQNdp/view?usp=sharing, which meets the seven-slide limit in the Project Submission Guide. The 2 min 58 s screen recording on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP3VFS-zw9M is an extended walkthrough prepared for LOCAL JUDGING ONLY: the local organiser confirmed on 15 November 2026 that this local event accepts a demo video of up to three minutes and asked for slides as well. That film is not the submitted Project Demo and is offered only as supplementary context for the local panel. Both files are held in a public Google Drive folder at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1pR8AYKUDQRy1YRYs-R_8QKqBIRhesh6m?usp=sharing - no sign-in and no access request. The closing page of the PDF links the live app, the public source repository, the film and the folder.
dataRefs: NASA POWER - monthly point API (all eight signals)
NASA GIBS - Blue Marble basemap + MODIS Terra true colour
MERRA-2 reanalysis (NASA GMAO, served via POWER)
CERES SYN1deg - satellite radiation and cloud, 2001-2025: the tested era (NASA LaRC, served via POWER)
GEWEX SRB - satellite radiation and cloud, 1991-2000: fetched but excluded from the trend test (NASA LaRC ASDC, served via POWER)
